questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Equation of a Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=4\sqrt[3]{x}.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4\sqrt[3]{x}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt[3]{x}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/3}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{3}{x}^{-2/3} \\  & =\frac{4}{3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(8)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(8) & =\frac{4}{3\sqrt[3]{{8}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3\sqrt[3]{64}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3\cdot 4} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=\frac{1}{3}$ and the coordinates of our point $(8,8),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-8 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-8) \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{8}{3}+8 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y={x}^{2}-3x$ at the point $(-2,10).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{2}-3x.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-3x)=2x-3.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(-2)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-2)=2(-2)-3=-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=-7$ and the coordinates of our point $(-2,10),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(10) & =-7(x-(-2)) \\ y-10 & =-7(x+2) \\ y & =-7x-14+10 \\ y & =-7x-4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y={x}^{2}-6x$ at the point $(3,-9).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{2}-6x.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-6x)=2x-6.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(3)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(3)=2(3)-6=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=0$ and the coordinates of our point $(3,-9),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-9) & =0(x-3) \\ y & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=5{x}^{2}+4x$ at the point $(1,9).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=5{x}^{2}+4x.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{x}^{2}+4x)=10x+4.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=10(1)+4=14\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=14$ and the coordinates of our point $(1,9),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(9) & =14(x-1) \\ y & =14x-14+9 \\ y & =14x-5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}+7x$ at the point $(1,9).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}+7x.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}+7x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{-5}+7x) \\  & =-10{x}^{-6}+7.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=-10(1{)}^{-6}+7=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=-3$ and the coordinates of our point $(1,9),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(9) & =-3(x-1) \\ y & =-3x+3+9 \\ y & =-3x+12.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find where the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{x}+\frac{6}{\sqrt{x}}$ at the point  $(4,5)$ intersects the $y$-axis.

The tangent intersects the $y$-axis at
$($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\sqrt{x}+\frac{6}{\sqrt{x}}.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x}+\frac{6}{\sqrt{x}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x})+6\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/2})+6\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}+6\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}){x}^{-3/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={f}^{′}(4) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{{4}^{3}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{3}{8} \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-5 & =-\frac{1}{8}(x-4) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{8}x+\frac{1}{2}+5 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{8}x+\frac{11}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $y$-axis, we set $x=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{8}(0)+\frac{11}{2} \\ y & =\frac{11}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(0,\frac{11}{2}).$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining where a Tangent Line Intersects an Axis
questions.problem:
Find where the tangent to the curve $y=-2\sqrt{x}$ at the point  $(4,-4)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The tangent intersects the $x$-axis at
$($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=-2\sqrt{x}.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-2\sqrt{x}) \\  & =-2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x}) \\  & =-2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/2}) \\  & =-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={f}^{′}(4) \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-4) & =-\frac{1}{2}(x-4) \\ y+4 & =-\frac{1}{2}x+2 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{2}x+2-4 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{2}x-2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}x-2 & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =-2 \\ x & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(-4,0).$

questions.problem: Find where the tangent to the curve  $y=\frac{5}{x}-2x$ at the point $(1,3)$ intersects the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{5}{x}-2x.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5}{x}-2x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{x}^{-1}-2x) \\  & =-5{x}^{-2}-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=-5(1{)}^{-2}-2=-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(3) & =-7(x-1) \\ y & =-7x+7+3 \\ y & =-7x+10.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $x=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-7(0)+10 \\ y & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(0,10).$

questions.problem:
Find where the tangent to the curve $y=4x-{x}^{2}$ at the point  $(1,3)$ intersects the $y$-axis.

The tangent intersects the $y$-axis at
$($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=4x-{x}^{2}.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4x-{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\  & =4-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=4-2(1)=2.
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-3 & =2(x-1) \\ y & =2x-2+3 \\ y & =2x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $y$-axis, we set $x=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2(0)+1 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(0,1).$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining where a Tangent Line Intersects an Axis
questions.problem:
Find where the tangent to the curve $y=\frac{2}{x}+x$ at the point  $(2,3)$ intersects the $y$-axis.

The tangent intersects the $y$-axis at
$($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{2}{x}+x.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{x}+x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{x})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{-1})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =-2{x}^{-2}+1 \\  & =-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={f}^{′}(2) \\  & =-\frac{2}{{2}^{2}}+1 \\  & =-\frac{2}{4}+1 \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-3 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-2) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x-1+3 \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $y$-axis, we set $x=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}(0)+2 \\ y & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(0,2).$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y = 2x^3 - 2x$ at the point $(1,0).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3 - 2x.$ Computing the derivative $f'(x)$ gives

$$
f'(x)  = 6x^2-2.
$$

We then compute $f'(1)$, which gives

$$
f'(1)  = 6(1)^2-2 = 4.
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=4$ and the coordinates of our point $(1,0),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =4(x-1) \\ y & =4x-4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find where the tangent to the curve $y=4\sqrt{x}+4x$ at the point $(1,8)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=4\sqrt{x}+4x.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4\sqrt{x}+4x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{1/2}+4x) \\  & =2{x}^{-1/2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
m=f'(1) = 2(1)^{-1/2}+4 = 6.
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-8 & =6(x-1) \\ y & =6x-6+8 \\ y & =6x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =6x+2 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $\left(-\dfrac 1 3, 0\right).$
